articles.title: The Cones That Wait for Fire
articles.dek: In 1988, a third of Yellowstone burned and the world mourned a dead forest. What grew out of the ash helps explain why Peter told suffering Christians that the fire was no stranger.
articles.quote: Fire is no stranger in the life of faith, because the Creator who planted you already knows what the heat will open.
articles.body:
In the summer of 1988, Yellowstone National Park caught fire. It was the driest summer anyone there had recorded, and lightning strikes plus a few careless human sparks grew into blazes that merged across the high country faster than crews could follow. By late summer about 25,000 firefighters had been sent into the region. On August 20, a day the rangers later called Black Saturday, the wind drove the flames across roughly 150,000 acres in a single day. Families watched the evening news as smoke rose over America's oldest national park, and more than one reporter spoke of Yellowstone as though it had died. When snow finally fell in September and smothered the last of it, more than a third of the park lay black.

Then the scientists walked into the ash. Ecologists such as Monica Turner spent years kneeling on the burned ground and counting what came up, and what came up astonished them. Within a few summers, lodgepole pine seedlings were rising through the charcoal, in some stands by the hundreds of thousands per acre. The explanation had been hanging in the branches all along. Many lodgepole pines carry what botanists call serotinous cones, sealed tight with a hard resin that can hold seeds safely for years. An ordinary warm afternoon will never open them. It takes heat of roughly 45 to 60 degrees Celsius to melt that seal, and a forest fire supplies it. The flames that blackened the trunks released the seeds, and the ash laid down a sunlit, mineral-rich bed for them to grow in. In a real sense, the forest had been built with this fire in mind.

Anyone who has lived through a season like that knows how the black ground looks the morning after. It may be a diagnosis, or a family that turned cold the year you started taking Jesus seriously. The Apostle Peter wrote one of the most tender passages in the New Testament to people standing in exactly that kind of ash.

His letter went out to "God's elect, exiles scattered throughout the provinces of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia" (1 Pet 1:1), the rugged interior of what is now Turkey. Picture one of those first readers, a young woman in a Bithynian market town. Before she met Christ, she went where everyone went: the temple feasts, the drinking nights of her husband's trade guild, the festivals where the whole town ate meat offered to the local gods. Now she stays home, and the town has noticed. Peter describes her neighbors precisely: "They are surprised that you do not join them in their reckless, wild living, and they heap abuse on you" (1 Pet 4:4). Customers drift to another stall. Her in-laws speak to her in short sentences. Rumors circulate, as they did across the empire, that Christians were secretive and disloyal and hated the gods who kept the city safe. One Sunday evening, in a crowded house lit by oil lamps, someone unrolls a letter from Rome and begins to read it aloud.

The man who wrote it knew fire personally. On the night Jesus was arrested, Peter stood warming his hands at a charcoal fire in a courtyard and denied three times that he knew him (John 18:18). Many scholars date this letter to the early 60s, not long before Nero turned on the Christians of Rome after the great fire of AD 64, and early church tradition holds that Peter himself died there under Nero. When he writes about suffering, he writes as a man who has failed in the heat, been restored by Jesus, and is about to walk into the heat again. Here is what he tells that young woman in Bithynia:

"Dear friends, do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal that has come on you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice inasmuch as you participate in the sufferings of Christ, so that you may be overjoyed when his glory is revealed." (1 Pet 4:12–13)

The word Peter uses for "surprised" in verse 12 is the Greek verb xenizō, from xenos, meaning foreign or alien. It is the same verb he used eight verses earlier for the neighbors who were "surprised" that the believers no longer joined them. One way to read this is that Peter is quietly turning the tables. Her town finds her new life strange, and that is to be expected, since she now belongs to another kingdom. The fire, however, should feel familiar to her, because it is the ordinary weather of everyone who follows a crucified Lord. Strangeness belongs to the watching world; familiarity belongs to the family of Jesus.

The phrase "fiery ordeal" translates pyrōsis, a word for the burning of a smelter's furnace. The ancient Greek translation of Proverbs 27:21 uses it for the furnace that tests gold, and Peter has already reached for that picture, calling faith "of greater worth than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire" (1 Pet 1:7). He adds a small phrase that carries enormous comfort: the fire has come "to test you." It has a purpose. It arrives inside the story God is telling, and it serves the moment "when his glory is revealed" (1 Pet 4:13). Peter even says that in these insults "the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you" (1 Pet 4:14), echoing the prophet's promise that the Spirit of the Lord would rest on the coming King (Isaiah 11:2). The heat that seems to signal God's absence is, in Peter's telling, the very place his presence settles.

Then comes the closing line of the chapter, and it reads as if Peter had walked through Yellowstone himself: "So then, those who suffer according to God's will should commit themselves to their faithful Creator and continue to do good" (1 Pet 4:19). This is the only place in the entire New Testament where God is called ktistēs, Creator. Peter could have chosen many titles, and in the hour of fire he chose the one that speaks of the God who designs living things and knows what each one needs to flourish. The word "commit" is paratithēmi, used for handing valuables to a trusted keeper for safekeeping. It is the word Jesus used from the cross: "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit" (Luke 23:46). The lodgepole pine does nothing clever in a fire. It simply holds what its Maker placed inside it, and the heat does what the Maker intended.

Much of our pain in hard seasons comes from the second burden we add to the first. Along with the illness or the rejection, we carry the question of whether God has stepped away, whether something has gone wrong in heaven's plans for us. Peter lifts that second burden off. He never pretends the fire is pleasant, and he never asks anyone to enjoy suffering for its own sake. He simply tells us that the fire is expected, that Christ has been in it before us, and that our Creator remains faithful while it burns. If you are facing such a season, you might take a few quiet minutes today to name it plainly before God and pray Peter's words over it: "Faithful Creator, I commit this to you." Then do one good thing for someone else before the day ends, because Peter pairs entrusting with continuing to do good, and the two belong together.

Today, nearly four decades after Black Saturday, young lodgepole forests stand thick and green across the slopes that once filled the television screens with smoke. The people who mourned in 1988 could see only the black ground, while the seeds were already loose in the ash. Fire is no stranger in the life of faith, because the Creator who planted you already knows what the heat will open. Whatever is burning around you this week, hold on to him, keep doing good, and watch the ground for green.

articles.title: Seven Years of Cooking Fires
articles.dek: In Ezekiel's vision, the weapons brought to destroy God's people end up as firewood in their kitchens. It may be the most homely picture of victory in the whole Bible.
articles.quote: What was carried in to destroy you can, in God's hands, become the fire that cooks tomorrow's rice.
articles.body:
In 1995, three years after Mozambique's long civil war had ended, an Anglican bishop named Dinis Sengulane saw a problem that no peace treaty could solve. The fighting had stopped, but the guns had stayed. Rifles lay buried in cassava fields, wrapped in plastic under floorboards and stacked in forgotten caches in the bush, and each one waited for a bad harvest or a family quarrel to put it back to work. So the bishop and the Christian Council of Mozambique started a project whose name came straight from the prophet Isaiah: Transforming Arms into Tools. A farmer could walk in carrying an assault rifle and walk home with a hoe on his shoulder. A former fighter could hand over a box of ammunition and leave with a bicycle, a sewing machine, or roofing sheets for his family's house.

Over the years that followed, hundreds of thousands of weapons were handed in. Many were cut apart and given to local artists, who welded the pieces into sculptures. One of them, a chair made entirely of decommissioned guns and called the Throne of Weapons, now sits in the British Museum in London. Any Filipino who grew up hearing a lola's old Singer humming in the corner of the sala knows what a sewing machine meant in a poor village. It meant school uniforms finished on time and a small income for the household. A thing built to end lives had been traded for a thing that kept a family going.

The prophet Ezekiel saw something very much like this, about twenty-six centuries earlier. Ezekiel was a priest taken to Babylon in 597 BC, and he spoke to exiles who had lost their land, their temple and, many of them feared, their God. When word came that Jerusalem had fallen (Ezekiel 33:21), his messages turned toward hope. God promised a new heart (36:26) and showed Ezekiel a valley of dry bones rising into a living army (37:10). Then, in chapters 38 and 39, comes a strange and sweeping vision. Long after the people have come home and settled into what the invader calls "a land of unwalled villages" (38:11), a ruler named Gog, "of the land of Magog" (38:2), gathers a vast coalition from the far north to swallow them whole. Scholars have long debated who Gog stands for, and wise readers hold their conclusions humbly. The text itself makes plain that he represents every power that ever looked at God's people and saw easy prey.

The battle takes only a few verses. God shakes the land, throws the invaders into such confusion that "every man's sword will be against his brother" (38:21), and pours down "hailstones and burning sulfur" (38:22). The great army falls on the mountains of Israel. And then the vision slows down and lingers on the aftermath, which turns out to be wonderfully ordinary.

"Then those who live in the towns of Israel will go out and use the weapons for fuel and burn them up: the small and large shields, the bows and arrows, the war clubs and spears. For seven years they will use them for fuel. They will not need to gather wood from the fields or cut it from the forests, because they will use the weapons for fuel. And they will plunder those who plundered them and loot those who looted them, declares the Sovereign LORD." (Ezekiel 39:9–10)

Ancient shields were made of wood and hide, bows were wood, and spears and clubs had wooden shafts, so the picture is physically believable. The Hebrew uses two plain household verbs, ba'ar and nasaq, the same words a woman would use for lighting the morning fire. Imagine a mother in a hill town stooping over her hearth every day for seven years and feeding the flames with the shaft of a spear that had been carried across the border to kill her children. The weapon arrived meaning harm, and it ends its life warming her bread.

One way to read this chapter is that God's victories are seldom finished on the day of the battle. The war in chapter 38 is over in an afternoon, but the healing in chapter 39 takes seven years of firewood and seven months of burial work, in which "all the people of the land will bury them" (39:13). They even bury the enemy dead with care, marking every bone so the land can be made clean (39:15). In Hebrew thought, seven is the number of completeness. God gives his people a full season to turn the leftovers of their fear into something useful, one cooking fire at a time, and he asks the whole community to do that work together.

The rest of Scripture keeps returning to this pattern. Isaiah dreamed of a day when nations "will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks" (Isaiah 2:4), the very verse that inspired the bishop in Mozambique. And long before either prophet, Joseph stood before the brothers who had sold him into slavery and said, "You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives" (Genesis 50:20). The betrayal that was supposed to finish him became, years later, the road by which he fed the very family that had wronged him.

Most of us will never see an army in our hills. Yet many of us carry weapons left behind by other people's attacks. There is the cutting remark from a parent that still replays at night, the officemate who took credit for our work, and the relative whose story about us traveled around the whole clan before the reunion. Filipinos know how long a family tampo can last. The natural instinct is to keep these things stacked in a back room, polished and ready, in case we ever need them again. Ezekiel offers a better use for them. Whatever has been hurled at us can be carried out into the open, handed to God, and burned as fuel for warmth.

This is what happens when a woman who was mocked for her accent becomes the gentlest mentor of shy new hires, or when a man who grew up with a harsh father makes his own home a place where children laugh freely. Their pain has gone into the fire and is warming other people. Such work is rarely quick. Ezekiel allows seven years, and grace is patient with people who need every one of them. Today you might name one old wound before God and ask him for a single way it could warm someone else, perhaps through a message to a friend who is walking through the same thing you once survived.

The chapter closes with God's tenderest words. His people "will forget their shame" when they live "in safety in their land with no one to make them afraid" (39:26), and God promises, "I will no longer hide my face from them, for I will pour out my Spirit on the people of Israel" (39:29). A fire on the hearth is the sign of a home where people are living again. That is the future God holds out, one where the enemy's shields become kindling and the rooms of your life fill with the smell of breakfast.

Somewhere in Mozambique tonight, a sewing machine traded for a rifle may still be humming. Let it remind you of what God is willing to do with your own story. What was carried in to destroy you can, in God's hands, become the fire that cooks tomorrow's rice.

articles.title: The Psalm of Buti Na Lang
articles.dek: Every Filipino family has a story that begins with a near miss. Psalm 124 teaches us how to finish that story, by saying out loud who was there.
articles.quote: Gratitude grows deepest when we dare to picture the night that never happened, and then say aloud who kept it from happening.
articles.body:
Sit long enough at any Filipino handaan, after the pancit has gone around twice and the children have drifted to the corner with their phones, and someone will start a story with two small words: buti na lang. Good thing. Tita Baby tells how she was booked on the early bus to Bicol, the one that later skidded off the road, and how she missed it only because she could not find her other slipper. Tito Ramon tells about the night the water in Marikina climbed to the second step of the stairs, then the third, and then simply stopped. Lola has heard these stories a hundred times, and she nods along until the end, when she adds the line she always adds: "Kung hindi dahil sa Diyos." If not for God.

The grandchildren roll their eyes a little, because they know every word. But something is being handed down at that table, and they will find it years later, when they stand in a hospital corridor of their own or watch a typhoon warning climb to Signal No. 4. The old stories come back to them then, carrying a quiet conviction: our family has been in trouble before, and we were carried through. Those after-dinner stories are among the most hopeful habits a Filipino home has, and few of us realize that the Bible contains a song built exactly the same way.

Psalm 124 belongs to a small collection called the Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120 to 134). Scholars widely understand these as songs that pilgrims sang while walking uphill to Jerusalem for the great yearly festivals, families and whole villages traveling together on dusty roads. This one carries the heading "Of David," and it reads like a song meant for a crowd. A leader begins, "If the LORD had not been on our side," and then stops to call out to everyone walking with him, "let Israel say" (Psalm 124:1). The people answer by repeating the line: "if the LORD had not been on our side when people attacked us" (Psalm 124:2). It is call and response, the way a family finishes a story everyone already knows.

Then the song paints what almost happened, and the pictures are vivid. Enemies are pictured as a beast that "would have swallowed us alive" (Psalm 124:3). Next comes water: "the flood would have engulfed us, the torrent would have swept over us, the raging waters would have swept us away" (Psalm 124:4–5). Anyone who lived in ancient Israel knew the danger of the wadi, a dry gully that could become a roaring river within minutes when winter rain fell in the hills, sweeping away travelers who had camped in the low ground. Filipinos who have watched a calm creek turn brown and furious in an afternoon understand the image without explanation. The psalmist adds teeth for good measure (Psalm 124:6), and then, in the middle of all that danger, the song turns small and tender, settling on one little bird.

"We have escaped like a bird from the fowler's snare; the snare has been broken, and we have escaped." (Psalm 124:7)

The Hebrew word that opens this psalm is lûlê, a little particle meaning "if not" or "were it not for." It is the same feeling as Lola's "kung hindi dahil sa." What makes the psalm unusual is how much room it gives to that word. For five verses, David describes a disaster that never took place, the swallowing, the flood, the drowning. One way to read this is as a lesson in a kind of gratitude we rarely practice. Most of our thanksgiving is for things we can see: the job that came through, the healing, the passing grade. This psalm thanks God for what we were spared, and that is a much larger list, because most of our rescues happen without our ever knowing how close we came.

The bird in verse 7 deepens the picture. A fowler in the ancient world caught small birds with a net or a spring trap, often baited with seed and held open by a trigger stick. Once that trap closed, a sparrow had no strength to break the cords or the frame. The psalmist chooses his words carefully here: "the snare has been broken." He does not say the bird broke it. The verb is passive, and this suggests that someone else did the breaking. The bird's whole part in its own rescue was to fly once the way was open. Psalm 91:3 uses the same picture as a promise, "Surely he will save you from the fowler's snare," and Psalm 124 sings it as a memory of a promise already kept.

This is gentle news for anyone who feels trapped right now. Many of us believe that escaping a hard season depends on how hard we struggle against it, and so we wear ourselves out pulling at the cords. The psalm offers a softer picture. The breaking belongs to God, and our part is to stay ready, to keep our wings, and to fly when he opens the door. Sometimes that door is a phone call from a friend, a doctor's new suggestion, or a quiet morning when the heaviness lifts enough to pray again.

The song ends with a line that God's people have kept close for centuries: "Our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth" (Psalm 124:8). Many Reformed churches, following a practice going back to John Calvin's Geneva, still open their Sunday worship with these exact words. In Geneva itself, the people sang Psalm 124 in thanksgiving after the city survived a surprise night attack in December 1602, and they still remember that night every year. It is a lovely fit. The God who made the heavens made the very sky the freed bird flies into, so there is no place the bird can land that lies outside his care.

Our buti na lang stories, it turns out, are half of a psalm. We tell the near miss well, with all the details of the slipper and the bus and the rising water, and then we often stop before naming who was there. Psalm 124 asks us to finish the story. Tonight at dinner, or in a short message to a sibling or an old friend, you might tell one of your own family's rescue stories and end it the way Lola does, by saying plainly that God kept you. Children who hear that ending enough times grow up with a memory of faithfulness they can lean on when their own floods come.

And if you are still inside the trap this week, take heart from the way the pilgrims used this song. They sang it while still walking uphill, tired and dusty, with Jerusalem not yet in sight. They sang about past rescues so that they could keep climbing toward the next one. You can borrow their song the same way, saying over your own situation, "If the LORD had not been on my side," and letting the memory of what he has already done steady your steps today.

Gratitude grows deepest when we dare to picture the night that never happened, and then say aloud who kept it from happening. Somewhere in your history is a flood that stopped at the third step. Give thanks for it, tell it to someone you love, and trust that the same hands are working on the snare you are facing now.

articles.title: The Seat You Never Have to Grab
articles.dek: A proverb from Solomon's palace, later retold by Jesus at a crowded dinner, frees us from the tiring work of claiming our own place.
articles.quote: The person who knows where God has seated them can sit anywhere.
articles.body:
On the evening of November 13, 1861, Abraham Lincoln walked through the dark streets of Washington to the house of his top general, George B. McClellan. With him came Secretary of State William Seward and the president's young secretary, John Hay. The Civil War was going badly, the Union army sat idle, and Lincoln wanted to talk strategy with the man in charge of it. McClellan was out at a wedding, so the President of the United States sat down in the parlor to wait. About an hour later the general came home, was told who was waiting for him, and walked past the parlor door and up the stairs. Half an hour after that, a servant came down with a message: the general had gone to bed.

Hay was outraged. In his diary that night he called it the “unparalleled insolence of epaulettes,” and on the walk home he said so to his boss. Lincoln, Hay recorded, did not seem to have taken it personally, and said it was better at that time not to be making points of etiquette and personal dignity. According to another widely repeated account, Lincoln once said he would gladly hold McClellan's horse if the general would only bring the country victories. A year later McClellan was removed from command. Lincoln, of course, now sits in marble on the National Mall, and Filipinos who have never set foot in America still know his face. He had no way of knowing how the story would end on that cold night. He simply cared more about his country than about his chair in the parlor, and he let the slight pass without a fight.

That picture of a great man content to wait in the lesser seat is the very scene behind a small saying in Proverbs 25. The chapter opens with a note that is easy to skip: “These are more proverbs of Solomon, compiled by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah” (Proverbs 25:1). Around two hundred years after Solomon, the scribes of King Hezekiah gathered these sayings, and many of them read like a training manual for young men who would serve in a royal court. Verses 2 to 5 speak about kings and how a throne is made secure. Then, in verse 6, the writer turns to the ambitious young official walking into the king's banquet hall for the first time.

Picture that hall. The low tables are arranged by rank, and everyone knows it. The seats nearest the king belong to his trusted advisers, the great men of the realm, and a newcomer's eyes go straight to them. He has worked hard, he is gifted, and he is sure he deserves to be noticed. It would be so easy to drift toward the front, take one of those cushions, and hope no one objects. The old teacher, who has watched this happen many times, leans in and offers a warning.

“Do not exalt yourself in the king's presence, and do not claim a place among his great men; it is better for him to say to you, ‘Come up here,’ than for him to humiliate you before his nobles.” (Proverbs 25:6–7)

The Hebrew phrase translated “do not exalt yourself” is built from the word hadar, which means splendor or majesty. It is the word the psalmist uses when he says of God, “you are clothed with splendor and majesty” (Psalm 104:1). So the proverb says, quite literally, do not dress yourself in glory. Glory worn by your own hand is a borrowed costume, and in a king's court someone will always notice that it does not fit. The word for “humiliate” comes from a root meaning to make low, and the picture is painfully concrete: the host walks over, in front of everyone, and moves you down the table. Every Filipino who has felt hiya burn in their cheeks knows exactly how that walk to the back would feel.

About a thousand years later, Jesus was eating in the home of a prominent Pharisee on a Sabbath, and Luke tells us that “he noticed how the guests picked the places of honor at the table” (Luke 14:7). He watched the quiet scramble for the best seats, and then he retold this very proverb. “When you are invited, take the lowest place,” he said, “so that when your host comes, he will say to you, ‘Friend, move up to a better place.’ Then you will be honored in the presence of all the other guests” (Luke 14:10). Jesus kept the shape of the old saying and added one warm word to the host's invitation: Friend.

In both versions, honor comes through the host's voice. The guest can take a seat, but only the host can give one, and a seat that is given is the only kind that truly belongs to you. That is why the proverb is wiser than simple good manners. It teaches that our standing before a king is something we receive, and that the wise person spends their energy being faithful while leaving the seating chart to the one who owns the table.

The gospel takes this one step further, and it is where the passage becomes good news. Jesus did more than teach the lowest seat; he took it. Paul writes that Christ, “being in very nature God, did not consider equality with God something to be used to his own advantage; rather, he made himself nothing by taking the very nature of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7). The Son of God walked past every place of honor and sat down at the very bottom, at a criminal's cross. Then the Father spoke the words of Proverbs 25 over him: “Therefore God exalted him to the highest place” (Philippians 2:9). He was the guest who was told, “Come up here.”

Because we belong to him, that invitation has already reached us too. Paul says that “God raised us up with Christ and seated us with him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:6). Seated is a past-tense word. If you trust in Jesus, the King has already called your name and set out your place, and no one in any boardroom, family reunion, or church committee can move you down from it. Seen this way, humility stops being a clever tactic for getting ahead later and becomes a kind of rest. The person who knows where God has seated them can sit anywhere.

This frees us in ordinary places. Most of us know the little dance at Filipino weddings and fiestas, where everyone glances at the presidential table, and the quiet ache when our name is not called to the front with the ninongs and ninangs. We know the office version too, when someone else presents the project we stayed late to finish, and the online version, when we post and then check, again and again, who has noticed. In each of these moments the heart reaches for a cushion near the king. The proverb, read in the light of Christ, invites us to let go of it, because the seat that matters is already ours.

So at the next gathering, you might choose a chair near the back and let the host decide whether to call you forward. At your next meeting, you could name a colleague's contribution before you mention your own, and mean it. And when someone overlooks you, as McClellan overlooked Lincoln, you can let the slight pass, the way Lincoln did, trusting that your dignity is held safely in another's hands. Peter puts the promise simply: “Humble yourselves, therefore, under God's mighty hand, that he may lift you up in due time” (1 Peter 5:6).

You do not have to fight for your place today. The King of the banquet has already looked down the long table, found you there, and called you friend. Walk into every room with that settled joy, take the lower seat gladly, and let him be the one who says, in his own time, “Come up here.”
